The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MITCHELL

The young woman sat rigidly in the conference room chair, her fingers drumming an anxious rhythm on the polished table. She studied the grain of the wood, traced invisible patterns on its surface, and adjusted her collar three times in as many minutes.

"I've been offered the lead position on the first autonomous vehicle testing facility in the Martian colonies," she said.

The older woman across from her set down her tablet and regarded her thoughtfully. "It's remarkable, isn't it? The new atmospheric processors make it possible now. There was a time when we couldn't even dream of surface facilities."

The young woman looked frustrated.

"I don't think I want to accept," she said quickly. "I don't think I want to spend three years there."

The older woman leaned back in her chair and folded her hands. "You mean you'd miss Earth—the people you've worked with, the familiar routines that have shaped your career here. You're worried the excitement would fade and you'd grow to resent Mars."

The young woman nodded miserably. "Yes, exactly that."

"Is there something else?"

The young woman's fingers found the table grain fascinating again. Finally, in a barely audible voice: "Yes."

"Someone special?"

A slight nod confirmed this.

The older woman smiled gently. "You know, of course, that the Commission's position is that research facilities should eventually be staffed by committed partnerships. Once it becomes feasible."

"But that could take years!" the young woman protested.

"It could—but sometimes these things happen faster than expected. And the goal makes it worthwhile."

"I suppose, but—"

The older woman's smile deepened. "Still the reluctant innovators," she murmured.

---

Grace Osborne stared at the communications terminal.

Four years at this research station and they didn't want her to come back.

Four years developing autonomous vehicle systems for Martian terrain and they assumed she'd gladly stay longer. Just increase her compensation package, the standard corporate logic. They probably thought she'd found her calling here.

Sure, she loved it. Recycled water, protein paste, vitamin supplements, and filtered air until your body felt like a chemistry experiment. Life in a cramped habitat module where you could walk twenty paces before hitting a wall. Their glorious frontier outpost with none of Earth's comforts—a fascinating place where real showers were rationed, fresh food was a memory, and the low gravity played havoc with your bone density.

And for triple her salary they expected her to stay another two years. Maybe three. She should probably feel honored by the opportunity.

The terminal chimed again, demanding a response.

She typed: "Declined."

Silence, then an angry burst of text demanding reconsideration. Grace muted the notifications and turned toward the sleeping quarters.

The message hadn't woken anyone. They were all still asleep in their individual pods. Justin Wood, the geologist, was snoring peacefully in the lower tier. Zhang Williams, the poor kid assigned to stopover duty, was muttering in his sleep. Leo Potter wore that expression of perfect contentment, dreaming of home. Patrick Ford and David Rice lay perfectly still, sleeping lightly as always.

Lord, Grace thought, I'll be happy to see some different faces.

"What did they want?" Leo had one eye open, looking curious.

"They wanted me to stay until the next relief transport arrives," Grace whispered back.

"What did you tell them?"

She shrugged. "No."

"Diplomatic as always," someone else whispered. It was Patrick, sitting up in his pod. "If it were me, I'd have given them a detailed explanation of where they could file that request."

The others were stirring now, except for Zhang who had his back turned and seemed determined to sleep through everything.

Justin rubbed his face sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Somewhat. Who wouldn't be?"

"Don't take it personally. The board members have never been here. They don't understand what it's like. They're just trying to retain a valuable employee."

"Trying to retain a valuable employee," Grace said sarcastically. "They can keep trying."

"They think you've made a home here," Patrick said.

"Why don't you all shut up until morning?" Zhang was awake now, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't leaving today."

No, Grace thought, some of us aren't leaving. You aren't. And Martinez isn't either. Only Martinez isn't ever going back.

Leo pointed toward Zhang's pod, held a finger to his lips, and walked quietly to the small food preparation unit. It was his turn for breakfast duty.

The others began organizing their spaces, preparing for their last day of work at the station. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Fourth research group and they'd be on their way back to Earth.

And that includes me, Grace thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked to the one small observation window. It was morning—Mars's morning—and she suppressed a shiver. The Sun's rays were striking the far edge of Valles Marineris, casting long shadows across the rust-colored landscape. The rest was still shrouded in that peculiar Martian darkness, a jumble of red dust and jagged rock formations that made the Badlands look like paradise.

Two hundred meters from the habitat she could make out the small memorial cairn and the simple metal marker, constructed from spare parts and welded together. In the dim light, she could just read the station designation stamped at the top: "BW-1." Below that, the inscription they'd welded: "E. Martinez - She gave everything for science." You could still see the rover tracks in the fine dust where the group had gathered around it. That had been more than two years ago, but there was barely any wind to erase those tracks. They'd persist for decades.

That's what happened to people like Martinez, Grace thought. On Mars, one mistake could be your last.

Leo returned with the coffee. Grace took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to finish it. It had been in storage so long the flavor was more memory than reality.

Patrick was warming his hands on his cup, looking contemplative. Justin and David were pulling on their environment suits, getting ready to go outside. Zhang was still in his pod, trying to ignore them.

"Think we should check with the orbital station to see if they've departed yet?" Leo asked.

"I contacted them on the last call," Grace said. "The relief transport left twelve hours ago. They should arrive"—she checked her chronometer—"in about seven hours."

"Grace, you know, I've been thinking," Patrick said quietly. "You've been here twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do when you get back?"

It hit them then. Justin and David looked blank for a moment and slowly found equipment cases to sit on. The tops of their suits were still hanging on the wall rack. Leo lowered his coffee cup and looked serious. Even Zhang glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Grace said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think about it. None of us have. We've been like children waiting so long for something that we can't believe it when it's finally about to happen."

Leo nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here four years like you, but I understand what you mean." He warmed to the topic as the realization deepened. "What are you really going to do?"

"Nothing spectacular," Grace said, smiling. "I'm going to rent a place in Goldfield Village, get some actual music—not synthesized—and just watch real people living real lives. Then I think I'll visit someone."

"Who's the someone?" Patrick asked.

Grace grinned. "Just someone. What about you, Patrick?"

"Well, I'm going to be practical. First, I'll submit all my geological survey data to the Commission. Then I'm going to sell my story to a media production company and then—well, then I think I'll get properly drunk!"

Everyone laughed and Grace turned to Leo.

"How about you?"

Leo looked solemn. "Like Patrick, I'll fulfill my obligations to the expedition first. Then I'm going home to see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all expedition members had to be unattached," Patrick said.

"They are. And I understand the reasoning—professional ethics and all that. But who could pass up the compensation package the Commission offered?"

"If I had to do it again? Not me," Patrick said promptly.

They laughed. Someone said: "Play your music file, Grace. Today's the day for it."

The audio file was an old recording Grace had brought with her when she'd arrived with the First group. The quality was degraded from multiple copies, but the song was meaningful.

"Homeward Bound" by an ancient folk artist.

They played it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Grace thought. They were actually going home and the reality was starting to sink in.

"You know, Grace," Patrick said, "this station won't be the same without you. It's like you're the spirit of this place—we'll look at Mars from Earth and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the old movies," David said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

"Some home," Grace said. "The Greenwood Dreams Initiative talks about terraforming, about forests and lakes, but look outside. Nothing but black rock and red dust."

"Greenwood Dreams," Leo mused. "I remember reading about that proposal. They want to eventually create whole ecosystems here."

"Fifty years from now, maybe a hundred," Patrick said. "Right now, this place is about as far from green as you can get. The dark basalt formations outside look like charred wood. That's why we nicknamed the western ridge the 'burnt forest.'"

Grace nodded. "When I first arrived with the First group, I remember looking out at those black volcanic formations and thinking the whole landscape looked scorched. Like someone had taken a pristine wood and burned it to ash."

The others joined in the gentle teasing and Grace smiled. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done this. She had been here too long and resented it too much.

The mood quieted after a while and Justin and David finished suiting up. They still had atmospheric readings to take before they left. Patrick was right after them. There was a rock formation he wanted to sample and some strata he needed to photograph.

And time went faster when you kept busy.

Grace stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for breaches," she warned. "And verify your oxygen tank levels."

Patrick looked annoyed. "I've gone out at least seven hundred times," he said, "and you check me every single time."

"And I'd check you seven hundred more," Grace said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch for unstable ground. Step through one of those weak spots and that's it."

Patrick sighed. "Grace, you watch us like we're children. You verify our suits, you mediate our disputes, you ensure we're not bored and that we stay healthy and productive. I think you'd tie our shoes if we couldn't manage it ourselves. But someday, Grace old friend, you're going to discover that your team can handle themselves!"

But he checked his suit for breaches and verified his tank level before he left.

Only Leo and Grace remained in the habitat. Leo was at the work station, carefully cataloging some bacterial specimens.

"I never knew you were married," Grace said.

Leo didn't look up. "There wasn't much point in discussing it. You just end up dwelling on it and wanting—and there's nothing you can do. You talk about it and it just intensifies the longing."

"He let you go without objection?"

"No, he didn't object. But I don't think he wanted me to go, either." He laughed slightly. "At least I hope he didn't."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Grace?" Leo asked. "I know what we said earlier, but I mean genuinely."

Grace thought for a moment. "I think I miss the weather," she said quietly. "Real weather. Rain and snow and wind that isn't trying to kill you. Trees that change with the seasons. I think, when I get back, I'd like to stand in a thunderstorm and just feel the rain on my face."

She paused, feeling self-conscious. Leo's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go to a crowded place—maybe Eastwood in Prandoria—and just watch people. Or maybe go to a live performance and smell the popcorn and feel the energy of a real audience in the dark."

She examined her hands. "I think what I miss most is humanity in all its complexity—complexity science could never fully capture. All kinds of people. People struggling with applied ethics in their daily lives. People who wouldn't know strategic planning from urban planning. And people who wouldn't care. We're hundreds of millions of kilometers from everything familiar, Leo, and what I miss most is the messy, beautiful chaos of human society."

"Someone special back home?" Leo asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Zhang. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Leo sealed the specimen container. "Going to get married when you return?"

Grace was at the window again, staring out at the desolate landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down somewhere and build a life together?"

Grace nodded.

"That's the only real future," Leo said.

He stored the container and joined her at the window. Grace moved over so they could both look out.

"Grace." Leo hesitated. "What happened to Martinez?"

"She died," Grace said. "She was brilliant, completely dedicated to the research. Being on Mars was the opportunity of a lifetime. She was so focused on the work that she forgot the fundamentals—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second group arrived, she went out to complete some experiments. She forgot to check for suit breaches and whether her tank valve was fully closed. We couldn't reach her in time."

"She had her communicator?"

"Yes. It worked perfectly. We heard everything she was thinking at the end."

Leo's face was expressionless. "What's your real job here, Grace? Why does someone have to stay for stopover?"

"Many reasons, Leo. You can't bring in a whole relief crew and let them take over without guidance. They need to know where you left off. They need to know where equipment is, how systems work, what hazards to watch for. And because you've been here two years and understand the environment, you have to monitor them to ensure they stay alive despite their inexperience. Mars is a hostile environment and you have to learn how to survive in it. There's a lot to learn—and some people just never do."

"You're a caretaker, then."

"I suppose you could say that."

Leo said, "You're not a researcher, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the pilot and systems engineer of the first transport. We converted parts of the ship into the habitat, so there wasn't anything to return on. I'm good with machinery and made myself useful with the equipment. When it became clear someone would need to stay for stopover, I volunteered. I thought the others were so valuable that their data should get back to Earth when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Zhang will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Grace frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't considered that. I don't believe I care anymore. I've served my time; it's someone else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was clear in explaining the responsibilities when you all discussed it."

"You were, but I don't think Zhang's right for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look heroic. He doesn't have the judgment that someone older would have. That you have."

Grace turned slowly and faced Leo.

"I'm not irreplaceable," she said slowly, "and even if I were, it wouldn't matter to me. I'm sorry if Zhang is young. So was I. I've lost four years here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Leo held up his hands. "Look, Grace, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you resent it and the time you've invested. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a critically important job."

Leo had gone out for a final equipment check and Grace enjoyed one of her rare moments of solitude. She wandered to her pod and opened her personal storage locker. She checked her civilian clothes and toiletries for perhaps the hundredth time and pushed everything down further in the bag. It was unnecessary because the bag had been packed for a week. She remembered postponing it as long as possible and then the quiet satisfaction about a week ago when she had opened her locker and transferred its meager contents to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than a day she'd be back on Earth where she could buy more toothpaste than she could use in a decade. She could leave behind her worn clothes and the oversized shirts she had inherited from—who was it? Richardson?—from the First group. Zhang could probably use them or maybe someone from the Fourth.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks on the wall panel beside her pod. Just hours ago, when she woke, she had made the final mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Martinez's.

She frowned thinking about Martinez and secured the bag's closure. They should never have sent someone like Martinez to Mars.

She had just locked the bag when she heard the airlock cycle and the soft hiss of equalization. Someone had returned earlier than expected. She watched the inner door open and the suited figure enter and remove its helmet.

Zhang. He had gone out to assist Justin with the atmospheric sensors. Maybe Justin hadn't needed help, with David along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Zhang wasn't much help to anyone today.

Zhang stripped off his suit. His face was covered with perspiration and his eyes showed fear.

He moistened his lips. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports more frequently than every two years, Grace? I mean, considering the advances in—"

"No," Grace interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not for at least a decade. The fuel costs too much and the journey's too dangerous. In terms of transport economics, you're worth more than your weight in platinum when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, it won't shorten stopover periods right away." She paused, feeling some sympathy for Zhang. "It won't be terrible. There'll be new people here and you'll spend considerable time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Zhang started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to talk to you about stopover. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be searching for the right words. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Grace, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and produced a photograph, placing it on the work station. "That's a picture of Alex, taken at a gathering we attended together." Grace didn't look. "We—I—expected to get married when I returned. I never told Alex about stopover, Grace. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that somehow—"

He was handling it badly, Grace thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Zhang? You thought I might stay for stopover again, in your place?"

It hurt to see Zhang's eyes. They were the eyes of someone desperately trying to stop themselves from doing something shameful, but unable to help themselves.

"Well, yes, essentially. Oh, God, Grace, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Zhang looked as though he might be sick. Grace tried to recall everything she knew about him. Zhang Williams. Excellent engineer. Graduate from a prestigious technical institute. Family was involved in natural resource management or something similar.

It still didn't quite add up. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Grace said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Zhang took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too desperate to remember pride, "you know my family's quite well-off. We would make it worth your while, Grace." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Grace, but they'd be well-compensated years!"

Grace felt exhausted. The good feeling about going home was slowly dissolving.

"If you have any reports to complete, I think you should get started," she cut in, keeping the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport departs. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Earth from here."

She felt more sympathy for Zhang than she could remember feeling for anyone. Long after returning home, Zhang would remember this moment.

It would haunt him.

Cowardice is the one thing no one ever forgives themselves for.

Patrick was eating a nutrition bar and looking out the window, so naturally he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We have visitors!" He rushed for his suit. Justin and David followed quickly and all three headed for the airlock.

Grace was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said quietly. "Just be certain to check."

"Oh, come on, Grace!" Patrick started angrily. Then he stopped and went over his suit. He got to his tank and went pale. Nearly empty. It was only a kilometer to the relief transport, so someone probably would have reached him in time, but.... He bit his lip and got a full tank.

Grace and Leo watched them cross the Martian surface, making the long, bounding strides that low gravity permitted. The transport's hatch had opened and small figures were descending the ramp. The figures from the habitat reached them and performed a brief dance of welcome. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Grace noticed one—probably Patrick—pat the transport's hull affectionately before starting back.

They were in the airlock and the air cycled in and then they were in the habitat, removing their suits. The newcomers were impressed and serious, acutely aware of the tremendous responsibility that now rested on them. Like Patrick and Leo and the members of the Second group had been when they arrived. Like Grace had been with the First.

Patrick and the others surrounded them.

How was Earth? What was the political situation? Were the autonomous vehicle regulations finally passed? What was happening in healthcare policy? Was the orbital station expansion complete?

Was the sky still blue, was the grass still green, did the seasons still change, did people still love and argue and were there still people who didn't understand complexity science and didn't care?

Grace had experienced this before. But was Jordan still Jordan?

Some of the Fourth group members had brought personal items. One of them—a sturdy, enthusiastic woman named Camila Cook—was opening a container about thirty centimeters square and fifteen centimeters deep. Grace watched curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Leo said. "Hey, everyone, look at this!"

Grace and the others crowded around and suddenly Patrick leaned over and inhaled deeply. In the container, covering a thick layer of actual soil, was a small plot of living grass. They looked at it, awed. Leo reached out and touched it gently.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Grace carefully plucked a single blade and held it to her nose. It had been years since she had seen grass, experienced the luxury of walking barefoot on it and lying on its cool surface during those warm summer evenings when it was too pleasant to be indoors.

Camila blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and perhaps use the grow lights occasionally. Couldn't resist bringing it; it seemed like a symbol of something...." She looked embarrassed. "My sister works for the Greenwood Dreams Initiative, actually. She insisted I bring a piece of what they're working toward. A promise of what Mars might become."

Grace understood. If she had been thinking clearly, she should have tried to bring something like that instead of her music files.

"That's expensive grass," Zhang said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, it's worth about a thousand credits per blade?"

Camila looked distressed and someone said, "Oh, shut up, Zhang."

"Greenwood Dreams," Patrick murmured, touching the grass. "They should see the black basalt outside. It'll take centuries before anything green survives out there."

"That's why we're here," Camila said defensively. "Every research station is a step toward that future. Even this one, built on those dark volcanic plains."

One of the newcomers separated from the group and approached Grace. He extended his hand and said, "My name's Joshua Fuller. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Grace nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Fuller looked every inch a captain. Strong features, graying hair, the confident bearing of someone accustomed to command.

"You could say I'm in charge here," Grace said.

"Well, look, Ms. Osborne, is there somewhere we can speak privately?"

They walked to one corner of the habitat. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Grace said. "What's on your mind?"

Fuller found an equipment case and sat down. He looked at Grace carefully.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time at BW-1 than anyone else," he began.

"BW-1?"

"Sorry—that's what we call it in the transport manifests. The designation." He gestured vaguely at the walls. "The Commission's been considering giving it a proper name, actually. Something more inspiring. I heard someone suggest 'Greenwood Station'—in honor of the terraforming initiative, what Mars might become someday."

Grace shook her head. "They shouldn't. Look outside at those formations—the black volcanic rock, the charred-looking ridges. The original survey team named this site for what it looked like, not for dreams of the future. We're built on the edge of what we call the 'burnt forest'—square kilometers of dark basalt pillars that look like the remains of a fire that consumed everything. The name should reflect reality, not fantasy."

Fuller nodded slowly. "The original designation, then. I understand you wanted to see me for more than just curiosity."

Fuller reached for a container of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Grace gestured toward Zhang. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. He put the container away. "You know we have extensive plans for the station," he said.

"I hadn't heard specifics."

"Oh, yes, extensive plans. They're developing automated cargo transports now that could deliver building materials for additional habitat modules. Enable us to expand the facility, have a series of modules all connected. Create proper laboratories and living quarters for the research staff." His eyes swept the room. "Provide some actual privacy for a change."

Grace nodded. "They could use some privacy here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak with you, Osborne. The Commission discussed it and they'd like you to stay. They feel if they're going to expand operations, add more modules and increase staff, that someone with practical experience should be managing things. They believe you're the only person who's capable and who has the necessary experience."

The captain vaguely sensed his approach was wrong.

"Is that everything?"

Fuller looked uncomfortable. "Naturally you'd be well compensated. I don't imagine anyone would enjoy being here indefinitely. They're prepared to triple your salary—perhaps even add a substantial bonus—and give you complete authority. You'd be Director of the research complex. Lead the expansion from this dark, barren outpost into something worthy of the dreams Camila's sister has—a real foothold for humanity on Mars."

All this and a title too, Grace thought.

"That's it?" Grace asked.

Fuller frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was additional compensation or...."

"The answer is no," Grace said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid you'd have to live here to appreciate that.

"Zhang Williams is staying for stopover. If there's something important about the project or upcoming changes, perhaps you should brief him before you leave."

She walked away.
